question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{1 - 49 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=7 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=7,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{7})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{1 - 49 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= 7\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(7 x)^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 7(\frac{1}{7})\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 1\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C \\  &= \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(7 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{49 - x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First factor the constant in the denominator:

$$
\sqrt{49 - x^{2}}=\sqrt{49(1-(\frac{1}{49})x^{2})}
$$

Use the linear substitution $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{7},\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(7)\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{49 - x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= \frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\frac{x}{7})^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= \frac{1}{7}(7)\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 1\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C \\  &= \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(\frac{x}{7} \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
\int \frac{6}{\sqrt{49 - 10 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First factor the constant in the denominator:

$$
\sqrt{49 - 10 x^{2}}=\sqrt{49(1-(\frac{10}{49})x^{2})}
$$

Use the linear substitution $u=\frac{\sqrt{10} x}{7}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{7},\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{7 \sqrt{10}}{10})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6}{\sqrt{49 - 10 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= \frac{6}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\frac{\sqrt{10} x}{7})^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= \frac{6}{7}(\frac{7 \sqrt{10}}{10})\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{10} \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}}{5}+C \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{10} \operatorname{arcsin}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{10} x}{7} \right)}}{5}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int \frac{12}{|12 x|\sqrt{(12 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=12 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=12,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{12})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

The substitution factor is positive, so the absolute values satisfy

$$
|u|=|12 x|=12|x|,\qquad \frac{1}{|x|}=\frac{12}{|u|}.
$$

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{12}{|12 x|\sqrt{(12 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= 12\int \frac{1}{|12 x|\sqrt{(12 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 12(\frac{1}{12})\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 1\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C \\  &= \operatorname{arcsec}{\left(12 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

This antiderivative applies on either interval where $|12 x|>1$; the constant may differ between those intervals.

question.:question/problem:

$$
\int \frac{6}{|x|\sqrt{49 x^{2} - 1}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=7,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{7})\,\mathrm{d}u.

$$
|u|=|7 x|=7|x|,\qquad \frac{1}{|x|}=\frac{7}{|u|}.

\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6}{|x|\sqrt{49 x^{2} - 1}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= 42\int \frac{1}{|7 x|\sqrt{(7 x)^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 42(\frac{1}{7})\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 6\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 6 \operatorname{arcsec}{\left(u \right)}+C \\  &= 6 \operatorname{arcsec}{\left(7 x \right)}+C\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{14}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{1 - 49 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the linear substitution $u=7 x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=7,\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{1}{7})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Change both bounds using the same substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=(7)(0)=0 \\ x=\frac{1}{14}&\Longrightarrow u=(7)(\frac{1}{14})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Both transformed endpoints lie strictly between $-1$ and $1$, so the integrand is continuous throughout the interval.

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{14}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{1 - 49 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= 3\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{14}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(7 x)^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= 3(\frac{1}{7})\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{3}{7}\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{3}{7}[\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \\  &= \frac{3}{7}(\operatorname{arcsin}(\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}(0)) \\  &= \frac{3}{7}((\frac{\pi}{6})-(0)) \\  &= \frac{\pi}{14}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{2}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{49 - x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First factor the constant in the denominator:

$$
\sqrt{49 - x^{2}}=\sqrt{49(1-(\frac{1}{49})x^{2})}
$$

Use the linear substitution $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{7},\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(7)\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Change both bounds using the same substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=(\frac{1}{7})(0)=0 \\ x=\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=(\frac{1}{7})(\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Both transformed endpoints lie strictly between $-1$ and $1$, so the integrand is continuous throughout the interval.

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{0}^{\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{2}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{49 - x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= \frac{3}{7}\int_{0}^{\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\frac{x}{7})^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= \frac{3}{7}(7)\int_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 3\int_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= 3[\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}]_{0}^{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\  &= 3(\operatorname{arcsin}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}(0)) \\  &= 3((\frac{\pi}{3})-(0)) \\  &= \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral. Give an exact answer.

$$
\int_{\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{4}}^{\frac{7}{2}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{49 - 2 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

{{answer}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First factor the constant in the denominator:

$$
\sqrt{49 - 2 x^{2}}=\sqrt{49(1-(\frac{2}{49})x^{2})}
$$

Use the linear substitution $u=\frac{\sqrt{2} x}{7}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{7},\qquad \mathrm{d}x=(\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{2})\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

Change both bounds using the same substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{4}&\Longrightarrow u=(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{7})(\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{4})=\frac{1}{2} \\ x=\frac{7}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{7})(\frac{7}{2})=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Both transformed endpoints lie strictly between $-1$ and $1$, so the integrand is continuous throughout the interval.

Apply the basic inverse-trigonometric integral:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}+C.
$$

Substitute and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{4}}^{\frac{7}{2}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{49 - 2 x^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x &= \frac{3}{7}\int_{\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{4}}^{\frac{7}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(\frac{\sqrt{2} x}{7})^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x \\  &= \frac{3}{7}(\frac{7 \sqrt{2}}{2})\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^{2}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}[\operatorname{arcsin}{\left(u \right)}]_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{arcsin}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}(\frac{1}{2})) \\  &= \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}((\frac{\pi}{4})-(\frac{\pi}{6})) \\  &= \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{8}\end{aligned}
$$
